transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-27
Time: 15:30 UTC (scheduled 45m — ran long)
Duration: 54 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Alicia Chen (Redwood AE), Marcus Patel (Redwood SE), Dr. Lena Ortiz (Solace Health - Head of Data Governance), Rajiv Menon (Solace - Platform Eng), Sofia Ibarra (Solace - Security & Compliance), Tomás Ruiz (Clinical Ops)

Summary:
Quick discovery to understand Solace Health's data residency constraints, HIPAA boundary needs, and how Redwood hosted vs dedicated vs private could map to their evidence collection and geofencing fallback policies. High level asks: region lock (EU vs US), keystore residency, log redaction/pseudonymization, audit events and retention, and performance/latency SLOs for clinical inference. They are leaning to private but want proof points and an architecture sketch.

Topics covered:
- Current infra and where PHI touches the stack
- Keystore residency and KMS/HSM preferences
- Log retention, redact vs minimize, and audit evidence packaging
- Geofencing and automatic regional fallback when primary region unavailable
- Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs (cost vs evidence and speed)

Action items (as captured on call): see metadata above.

Transcript:
[00:00] Alicia Chen: Hey everyone — thanks for joining, really excited to talk through your residency and compliance boundaries. Quick roll call — I can do quick context on Redwood and Marcus will field the deeper architecture bits.
[00:12] Dr. Lena Ortiz: Hi, thanks. We have limited time so we'll jump in. I'm Lena, I lead data governance at Solace Health. Our core question is how PHI stays in-region — we have EU patients and US patients and we need clear boundaries.
[00:25] Rajiv Menon: Rajiv here. I run the platform stuff — our main constraint is we can't send raw clinical notes outside of EEA for EU patients, and audit logs need to be immutable and retained for seven years for certain flows.
[00:40] Marcus Patel: Perfect, thanks. To start: Redwood offers Hosted (multi-tenant), Dedicated (reserved GPU pools), and Private (VPC/private control plane). Each has different guarantees on data egress and proofs of residency. We typically do region-locking and can restrict model serving to specific hardware pools.
[00:55] Sofia Ibarra: When you say "proofs of residency" — we need evidence for auditors: where keys live, where telemetry/logs are stored, and chain of custody for inference requests that touch PHI.
[01:12] Alicia Chen: Totally. We have SOC 2 and HIPAA artifacts we can share — the whitepaper covers our certs and the private deployment pack shows keystore options. We'll attach that after the call.
[01:24] Tomás Ruiz: From clinical ops, latency matters — if you lock to EU region we need sub-300ms 95th for the small classification model, can you hit that on Private?
[01:38] Marcus Patel: It depends on the hardware and batch configs — on Dedicated or Private with NVidia H100 or A100 class we can meet that, but we need to tune batching & KV cache behavior. Also note that quantization affects accuracy, we should run a POC.
[01:55] Dr. Lena Ortiz: Two immediate technical constraints: 1) KMS must be EU-resident for EU patient data; 2) Logs sent to external analytics must be scrubbed of direct identifiers or pseudonymized.
[02:12] Rajiv Menon: On KMS we already use a cloud KMS per region (Azure Key Vault in eu-west, GCP in europe-west3), but our security team requires that customer-controlled keys never cross region boundaries. How does Redwood integrate with customer KMS?
[02:28] Marcus Patel: In Private we can integrate your KMS via our keystore provider abstraction; the control plane can be customer-managed and we can reference your key URIs — so keys never leave your region. On Dedicated we have options for customer-managed keys as well, but Hosted with shared KMS is harder for that strict residency.
[02:45] Alicia Chen: To be clear — Hosted is fastest onboarding but has limited keystore residency controls. Dedicated (reserved pools) allows VPC peering and customer KMS, and Private gives the strongest guarantees because you control the control plane.
[02:58] Sofia Ibarra: Ok. Next: logs. For audit we need full request/response traces for a sample period, but we also need redaction at ingest so PHI isn't persisted in analytics. Can Redwood do selective logging?
[03:15] Marcus Patel: Yes — we support field-level redaction and configurable retention. There are two levers: don't log sensitive fields at proxy time (recommended), or log and then apply redactors for downstream analytics. We can also pseudonymize with hashing salted by a region-specific secret — that secret can be customer-managed so mapping back requires the customer's key.
[03:36] Rajiv Menon: Does your default logging include prompts? We don't want patient notes sitting in logs.
[03:40] Alicia Chen: Default for Hosted logs some metadata and limited prompt previews for debugging; for compliance customers we turn that off and enable minimal telemetry only. We'll share the exact schema, Marcus can show examples.
[03:52] Marcus Patel: I'll add an example retention table. For HIPAA flows we recommend: zero prompt retention (or ephemeral caches with TTL < 1 min), event audit logs (request ID, model id, timestamp, routing decision, checksum) stored in your S3 or customer-managed storage region.
[04:12] Dr. Lena Ortiz: On geofencing — what happens on failover? If eu-west goes down do requests route to us-east? That's unacceptable for EU patients. We need a fallback policy that preserves residency and surfaces errors to the app.
[04:26] Marcus Patel: We support policy-based routing. You can define strict residency: "no cross-border fallback" which will return an explicit 523 or 451-style error. Or a relaxed fallback: route to a secondary EU region or to Dedicated pool in same jurisdiction. The platform also emits the routing decision in the trace so you can assert compliance.
[04:46] Rajiv Menon: We need an SLA on that behavior — if primary region is degraded, what's the expected stall vs error time? And will failover create any transient logging outside region?
[04:58] Marcus Patel: With Private deployment you control the nodes and failover is internal, so no cross-region egress. With Dedicated, failover policy can be set to only go to other reserved pools in the same geo. Hosted multi-tenant has global fallback options; if you choose strict residency we can disable cross-region failover. We'll document the exact telemetry emitted during incidents.
[05:14] Tomás Ruiz: You mentioned KV cache earlier. If inference uses a KV cache, does that cache store patient prefixes? We can't persist PHI in cache beyond ephemeral use.
[05:26] Marcus Patel: Good callout. We support encrypted KV caches with TTLs and optional encryption using customer keys. For PHI workflows we recommend not caching raw prefixes — instead cache derived tokens or embeddings that are irreversible, or set TTL to ephemeral. We can enforce that as a policy on the model route.
[05:48] Dr. Lena Ortiz: For auditors we'll need evidence for: where keys are held, where caches live, a list of audit events and access logs for the control plane. Does Redwood provide signed evidence bundles?
[05:58] Alicia Chen: We can package evidence — control-plane audit logs, deployment manifests, and keystore access records. For Private deployments that's straightforward since you host the control plane. For Dedicated we can provide signed entries and access logs; for Hosted we provide tenant-separated logs but not the raw control-plane events.
[06:16] Rajiv Menon: Is there an automated export we can feed into our compliance pipeline? We want to ingest logs into our SIEM (Splunk) and have them land in our EU Splunk instance.
[06:27] Marcus Patel: Yes. We provide log sinks to customer-managed cloud storage or direct ingestion endpoints. You can configure S3/Blob/GCS buckets in your region and we will push or you can pull.
[06:34] Sofia Ibarra: Encryption at rest and in transit — we require TLS 1.3 for transit and AES-256 for rest with customer-controlled keys. Can Redwood support that?
[06:45] Alicia Chen: Yes — TLS 1.3 and customer-managed KMS for Private and Dedicated. For Hosted we support encryption and TLS but customer-managed keys are only for certain tiers; we'll flag that in the doc.
[06:58] Tomás Ruiz: About deployment velocity — how long to stand up Private in our VPC? We have strict change windows and need an estimate.
[07:07] Marcus Patel: Typical Private deployment timeline is 4–8 weeks depending on network and security approvals: network setup (VPC, peering), KMS integration, private control plane install, and acceptance tests. We can accelerate with templates if your infra team can provide the VPC and KMS quickly.
[07:21] Dr. Lena Ortiz: For the POC we want to run a small model on EU-only data, validate latency, and confirm evidence flow. We also want to run a redaction test where we prove the logs don't contain PHI.
[07:33] Alicia Chen: Sounds good. Suggested POC: 2-week trial on Dedicated or Private with a restricted route, ingest a redacted dataset, run latency and quality checks, and capture audit evidence. We'll provide the POC success criteria template.
[07:45] Rajiv Menon: Pricing question — what's the delta between Dedicated and Private? We need a rough order of magnitude to budget.
[07:54] Alicia Chen: Dedicated is typically lower up-front and is reserved capacity; Private has additional platform fees plus some implementation cost because you control the control plane. I can send a pricing matrix and an example TCO spreadsheet.
[08:05] Sofia Ibarra: A few technical clarifications — can you support regional HSMs? And can the keystore access logs be immutably archived?
[08:16] Marcus Patel: Yes and yes. We support customer HSMs reachable from the deployed control plane; keystore access logs can be exported and written to WORM-enabled buckets. That can be part of the evidence bundle.
[08:30] Dr. Lena Ortiz: On consent and data minimization: we need to ensure the model outputs never echo patient identifying details; is there a guardrail for hallucination of PHI?
[08:42] Marcus Patel: We have a couple of levers: prompt sanitizers, model-level PII detection filters, and post-processing heuristics that redact high-confidence PHI strings. Those need evaluation in the POC because it can affect recall.
[08:59] Tomás Ruiz: Operational question — in an incident who from Redwood gets engaged and what's the timeline? We need an on-call escalation path.
[09:09] Alicia Chen: For Dedicated and Private customers we have an SLA with a named TAM and 24/7 incident response depending on tier. We'll include the escalation matrix in the doc pack.
[09:21] Rajiv Menon: Ok, last area: legal hold and export. If a regulator requests records for a subset of EU patients, can we produce the raw inference traces with chain of custody and ensure they never left EU?
[09:33] Marcus Patel: In Private yes, you own the control plane and can generate signed export bundles from your EU storage. For Dedicated we can produce signed audit entries and exports from your reserved storage region; for Hosted we can produce tenant logs but there are limitations on control-plane level artifacts.
[09:52] Dr. Lena Ortiz: Great. A follow-up: can you show an example evidence bundle? Even a sanitized one so we can review fields.
[09:58] Alicia Chen: Yes — Marcus will attach an example and we'll include routing traces, keystore access entries, and a sample log retention policy.
[10:08] Marcus Patel: I'll prepare it. Also, note some nomenclature differences — sometimes our docs call K-V cache "K-V cache" but auto-transcription may spell it K-V cash — just flagging because of audit language.
[10:20] (brief laughter)
[10:30] Dr. Lena Ortiz: Are there any regulatory constraints you can't operate under? For example, can you support air-gapped deployments?
[10:38] Marcus Patel: We can support air-gapped on-prem installs for Private deployments — that's a larger engagement (multi-month) but doable.
[10:46] Rajiv Menon: For the POC — we want to test redaction + residency + latency in EU, and prefer Dedicated as a first step to reduce friction. If that goes well we'll plan Private.
[10:58] Alicia Chen: That makes sense — Dedicated short POC, then Private for production. We'll include success criteria and a runbook for escalation.
[11:06] Tomás Ruiz: One last question — do you have any references in the healthcare vertical for similar deployments?
[11:12] Alicia Chen: Yes — we can share anonymized case studies where we ran private deployments for medtech and a regional health network — I'll include those links.
[11:20] Dr. Lena Ortiz: Good. Thanks — that's helpful.
[11:25] Alicia Chen: Ok quick recap and next steps: 1) we'll send SOC2/HIPAA + keystore notes by 2026-11-30; 2) Marcus will draft VPC architecture and sample log retention table by 2026-12-03; 3) schedule workshop week of 2026-12-07. Customer will share data flow and PII taxonomy by 2026-12-03. Anything to add?
[11:45] Rajiv Menon: Sounds good. Also please include sample evidence bundle.
[11:51] Marcus Patel: Will do.
[11:55] Sofia Ibarra: Thank you. We'll review and circle back.
[12:00] Alicia Chen: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up in email with the pack.
[12:05] (call ended)

Notes on transcription: occasional misheard phrases and punctuation, speaker turns collapsed for readability. Some product names abbreviated; logs and KV cache references may be misspelled in the raw transcript.
